text: Preferred Training Methods – If Receiving Training Subsidy When asked how they would prefer to train workers if financial support was available, more than 37% of contractors favored hands-on, practical training formats (i.e., on-the-job training), as shown in Figure 14. Figure 14. Training preferences This preference reinforces the importance of experiential learning in the trades. Training subsidy programs that pay for workers while they train, prioritize hands-on formats that allow workers to practice skills in realistic conditions, and provide opportunities for mentorship from experienced staff are likely to be most attractive to contractors. Why Companies Might Not Train Workers Despite recognizing the value of training, many contractors identified clear reasons their company might choose to not train workers, as shown in Figure 15. The high cost of training ranked as the top reason for 28% of respondents and the second-top reason for 32% of respondents. Top reasons a company might not train workers These concerns point to a risk: Investing in workers may feel risky if contractors are unsure that they can recover training costs through increased productivity, higher-quality work, or long-term retention. Thirty-seven percent of contractors reported “training is not needed” as the lowest rank (five out of five). In contrast, most contractors reported that at least 20% of employees at their company are not well trained (see Figure 10). Workforce programs that reduce these risks—for example, by lowering the cost of training—may help close the gap between interest in training and actual investment. 4.5 Employee Retention and Spin-Out Practices Contractors identified several common reasons workers leave their companies, shown in Figure 16. The most frequently cited causes included employees starting their own businesses (59%), retiring (55%), and leaving the industry (45%). These forms of turnover disrupt firms, particularly smaller firms, where role redundancy is less common. The high rate of retirements underscores the need to increase efforts in recruiting new workers and upskilling the incumbent workers to maintain a proficient workforce. It is also important to assess why employees may be leaving the industry and understand retention measures to prevent the loss of talent and industry knowlegde. 23 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Figure 16. Top three reasons workers leave a company A notable share of contractors reported that workers sometimes leave to start their own business, a phenomenon sometimes referred to as “spin-offs.” When asked how common it is for employees to leave and start their own business, 42% of contractors shared that it is sometimes common. Although this can be challenging for employers who invest in training, it also reflects the entrepreneurial nature of the trades and may contribute to a broader ecosystem of skilled contractors over time.
